etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English casten, from Old Norse kasta (“to throw, cast, overturn”), from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), of unknown origin.

Cognate with Scots cast (“to cast, throw”), Danish kaste (“to throw”), Swedish kasta (“to throw, cast, fling, toss, discard”), Icelandic kasta (“to pitch, toss”). In the sense of "flinging", displaced native warp.

The senses relating to broadcasting are based on that same term; compare -cast.

definitions.definition: (now somewhat literary) To throw. [from 13th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1590–1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Two Gentlemen of Verona”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Why then a Ladder quaintly made of Cords / To cast vp, with a paire of anchoring hookes, / Would serue to scale another Hero's towre […].

quote.citation: 1759–1767, [Laurence Sterne], The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman, volume (please specify |volume=I to IX), London:  […]  T. Becket and P. A. Dehondt, […], page 262:
quote.text: The more, an' please your honour, the pity, said the Corporal; in uttering which, he cast his spade into the wheelbarrow […].

definitions.definition: To throw forward (a fishing line, net etc.) into the sea. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Matthew iiij:
quote.text: As Jesus walked by the see off Galile, he sawe two brethren: Simon which was called Peter, and Andrew his brother, castynge a neet into the see (for they were fisshers) […].

definitions.definition: To throw down or aside. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: So she to Guyon offred it to tast; / Who taking it out of her tender hond, / The cup to ground did violently cast, / That all in peeces it was broken fond  […]

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 6:30:
quote.text: it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.

quote.citation: 1930 December 19, “Sidar the Madman”, in Time:
quote.text: Near Puerto Limon, Costa Rica, Madman, co-pilot and plane were caught in a storm, cast into the Caribbean, drowned.

quote.citation: 2009, Hilary Mantel, Wolf Hall, Fourth Estate, published 2010, page 316:
quote.text: Her bow is not to her liking. In a temper, she casts it on the grass.

definitions.definition: (of an animal) To throw off (the skin) as a process of growth; to shed the hair or fur of the coat. [from 15th c.]
(obsolete except in set phrases) To remove, take off (clothes). [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1822, “Life of Donald McBane”, in Blackwood's Magazine, volume 12, page 745:
quote.text: when the serjeant saw me, he cast his coat and put it on me, and they carried me on their shoulders to a village where the wounded were and our surgeons […].

quote.citation: 2002 March 2, Jess Cartner-Morley, “How to Wear Clothes”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: You know the saying, "Ne'er cast a clout till May is out"? Well, personally, I'm bored of my winter clothes by March.

definitions.definition: (nautical) To heave the lead and line in order to ascertain the depth of water.
(obsolete) To vomit.

quote.citation: 1601, Ben Jonson, Poetaster or The Arraignment: […], London:  […]  [R. Bradock] for M[atthew] L[ownes] […], published 1602, →OCLC, Act I, scene i:
quote.text: These verses […] make me ready to cast.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To throw up, as a mound, or rampart.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 19:48:
quote.text: Thine enemies shall cast a trench [bank] about thee.

quote.citation: 1881, John Kirby Hedges, The history of Wallingford‎[1], volume 1, page 170:
quote.text: Kenett states that the military works still known by the name of Tadmarten Camp and Hook-Norton Barrow were cast up at this time ; the former, large and round, is judged to be a fortification of the Danes, and the latter, being smaller and rather a quinquangle than a square, of the Saxons.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To throw out or emit; to exhale.

quote.citation: 1695 (first published), 1726 (final dated of publication) John Woodward, An Essay toward a Natural History of the Earth and Terrestrial Bodies
quote.text: This […] casts a sulphurous smell.

quote.citation: 1849, Philip Henry Gosse, Natural History:
quote.text: This horned bird, as it casts a strong smell, so it hath a foul look, much exceeding the European Raven in bigness

definitions.definition: (physical) To move, or be moved, away.
To direct (one's eyes, gaze etc.). [from 13th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1591–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Third Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: To whom do Lyons cast their gentle Lookes? Not to the Beast, that would vsurpe their Den.

quote.citation: 1813 January 27, [Jane Austen], chapter 11, in Pride and Prejudice: […], volume I, London:  […]  [George Sidney] for T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: She then yawned again, threw aside her book, and cast her eyes round the room in quest of some amusement […].

quote.citation: 1959, Georgette Heyer, chapter 1, in The Unknown Ajax:
quote.text: But Richmond, his grandfather's darling, after one thoughtful glance cast under his lashes at that uncompromising countenance appeared to lose himself in his own reflections.

definitions.definition: (dated outside accounting) To add up (a column of figures, accounts etc.); cross-cast refers to adding up a row of figures. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1589–1590 (date written), Christopher Marlo[we], edited by Tho[mas] Heywood, The Famous Tragedy of the Rich Iew of Malta. […], London:  […]  I[ohn] B[eale] for Nicholas Vavasour, […], published 1633, →OCLC, Act I:
quote.text: To what this ten years' tribute will amount,That we have cast, but cannot compass itBy reason of the wars, that robb'd our store

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies. […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: The Clearke of Chartam: hee can write and / reade, and cast accompt.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 17, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book II, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: I cannot yet cast account either with penne or Counters.

quote.citation: 1719 May 6 (Gregorian calendar), [Daniel Defoe], The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, […], London:  […]  W[illiam] Taylor […], →OCLC:
quote.text: I cast up the notches on my post, and found I had been on shore three hundred and sixty-five days.

quote.citation: 1859, David Morier Evans, “The Royal British Bank—Its Suspension and General Mismanagement”, in Facts, Failures and Frauds, London: Groombridge & Sons, page 337:
quote.text: They cast it up and found it agreed with the printed balance-sheet.

quote.citation: 2007, George Puttick, Sandy van Esch, “Auditing Revenue Transactions and Balances”, in The Principles and Practice of Auditing, →ISBN, page 637:
quote.text: Obtain an aged list of accounts receivable balances at the financial year end and use CAATs to cast and cross-cast the schedule and agree the total to the general ledger control account for accounts receivable.

quote.citation: 2023, “Procedures”, in Audit and Assurance, Kaplan Financial Limited, →ISBN, page 354:
quote.text: Obtain a list of individual customers with balances outstanding at the year end, cast this and agree it to the trade receivables account.

definitions.definition: (astrology) To calculate the astrological value of (a horoscope, birth etc.). [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: , vol.1, New York Review of Books, 2001, p.309:
quote.text: he is […] a perfect astrologer, that can cast the rise and fall of others, and mark their errant motions to his own use.

quote.citation: 1971, Keith Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic, Folio Society, published 2012, page 332:
quote.text: John Gadbury confessed that Mrs Cellier, ‘the Popish Midwife’, had asked him to cast the King's nativity, although the astrology claimed to have refused to do so.

quote.citation: 1985, Lawrence Durrell, Quinx, Faber & Faber 2004 (Avignon Quintet), p.1197:
quote.text: He did the washing up and stayed behind to watch the dinner cook while she hopped off with a friend to have her horoscope cast by another friend.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To plan, intend. [14th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1485, Thomas Malory, Le Morte Darthur Book XIX, Chapter i leaf 386v:
quote.text: [...] for the quene had cast to haue ben ageyne with kyng Arthur at the ferthest by ten of the clok / and soo was that tyme her purpoos.[...] "for the queen had cast to have been again with King Arthur at the furthest by ten of the clock, and so was that time her purpose."

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: I wrapt my selfe in Palmers weed, / And cast to seeke him forth through daunger and great dreed.

quote.citation: 1685, William Temple, "Upon the Gardens of Epicurus:
quote.text: The cloister […] had, I doubt not, been cast for [an orange-house].

definitions.definition: (transitive) To assign (a role in a play or performance). [from 18th c.]
(transitive) To assign a role in a play or performance to (an actor).
(transitive) To describe in an opinionated way. Mostly used with a metaphor involving light.
To consider; to turn or revolve in the mind; to plan.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 1:29:
quote.text: She […] cast in her mind what manner of salutation this should be.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To impose; to bestow; to rest.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: The government I cast upon my brother.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms 4:22:
quote.text: Cast thy burden upon the Lord.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To defeat in a lawsuit; to decide against; to convict.

quote.citation: 1822, John Galt, The Provost:
quote.text: She was cast to be hanged.

quote.citation: 1667, attributed to Richard Allestree, The Causes of the Decay of Christian Piety. […], London:  […]  R. Norton for T. Garthwait, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Were the case referred to any competent judge,  […] they would inevitably be cast.

definitions.definition: To turn (the balance or scale); to overbalance; hence, to make preponderate; to decide.

quote.citation: 24 July, 1659, Robert South, Interest Deposed, and Truth Restored
quote.text: How much interest casts the balance in cases dubious!

definitions.definition: (social) To predict, to decide, to plan.
To perform, bring forth (a magical spell or enchantment).

quote.citation: 1936, Rollo Ahmed, The Black Art, London: Long, page 178:
quote.text: Sorcery is not the exclusive prerogative of the fetish-man, but is practised haphazardly by anyone who wishes to cast a spell upon another.

definitions.definition: To throw (light etc.) on or upon something, or in a given direction.

quote.citation: 1950 April 24, “A Global View”, in Time:
quote.text: The threat of Russian barbarism sweeping over the free world will cast its ominous shadow over us for many, many years.

quote.citation: 1960, Lawrence Durrell, Clea:
quote.text: A sudden thought cast a gloom over his countenance.

quote.citation: 1972, “Thick As A Brick”, Ian Anderson (lyrics), performed by Jethro Tull:
quote.text: The Poet and the PainterCasting shadows on the waterAs the sun plays on the infantryReturning from the sea.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To give birth to (a child) prematurely; to miscarry. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: , Folio Society, 2006, vol.1, p.98:
quote.text: being with childe, they may without feare of accusation, spoyle and cast [translating avorter] their children, with certaine medicaments, which they have only for that purpose.

quote.citation: 1650, Thomas Browne, chapter V, in Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  A[braham] Miller, for Edw[ard] Dod and Nath[aniel] Ekins, […], →OCLC, 1st book, page 20:
quote.text: The abortion of a woman they describe by an horse kicking a wolf; because a mare will cast her foal if she tread in the track of that animal.

definitions.definition: (printing, dated) To stereotype or electrotype.
To shape (molten metal etc.) by pouring into a mould; to make (an object) in such a way. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1923 March 24, “Rodin's Death”, in Time:
quote.text: One copy of the magnificent caveman, The Thinker, of which Rodin cast several examples in bronze, is seated now in front of the Detroit Museum of Art, where it was placed last autumn.

quote.citation: 1944 November and December, A Former Pupil, “Some Memories of Crewe Works—II”, in Railway Magazine, page 343:
quote.text: The practice of casting steel seems the most difficult of all the foundry arts, for despite every care, a percentage of the work is liable to be faulty and disappointing, but at Crewe, generally, a very good class of casting was turned out.

definitions.definition: To twist or warp (of fabric, timber etc.). [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1680, Joseph Moxon, The Art of Joinery:
quote.text: Stuff is said to cast or warp when […] it alters its flatness or straightness.

definitions.definition: (nautical) To bring the bows of a sailing ship on to the required tack just as the anchor is weighed by use of the headsail; to bring (a ship) round. [from 18th c.]
To deposit (a ballot or voting paper); to formally register (one's vote). [from 19th c.]
(computing) To change a variable type from, for example, integer to real, or integer to text. [from 20th c.]
(hunting) Of dogs, hunters: to spread out and search for a scent. [from 18th c.]

quote.citation: 1955, William Golding, The Inheritors, Faber and Faber, published 2005, page 50:
quote.text: He clambered on to an apron of rock that held its area out to the sun and began to cast across it. The direction of the wind changed and the scent touched him again.

definitions.definition: (medicine) To set (a bone etc.) in a cast.
(Wicca) To open a circle in order to begin a spell or meeting of witches.
(media) To broadcast (video) over the Internet or a local network, especially to one's television.
An act of throwing.
The number rolled on a die when it is thrown.
(fishing) An instance of throwing out a fishing line.

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 152:
quote.text: I went out on the timber boom and made a few casts, but with little success.

definitions.definition: Something which has been thrown, dispersed etc.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Fourth Book of the Georgics”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: a cast of scatter'd dust

definitions.definition: A small mass of earth "thrown off" or excreted by a worm.
The collective group of actors performing a play or production together. Contrasted with crew.
The casting procedure.
An object made in a mould.
A supportive and immobilising device used to help mend broken bones.
The mould used to make cast objects.
(hawking) The number of hawks (or occasionally other birds) cast off at one time; a pair.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book VI, Canto VII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: As when a cast of Faulcons make their flight / An an Herneshaw, that lyes aloft on wing  […]

quote.citation: 2007, Tim Blanning, The Pursuit of Glory, Penguin, published 2013, page 395:
quote.text: Louis XIV was keen, employing a total hawking personnel of 175 and adding a fourth cast of gyrfalcons to hunt hares in 1682  […] .

definitions.definition: A squint.

quote.citation: 1847, John Churchill, A manual of the principles and practice of ophthalmic medicine and surgery, p. 389, paragraph 1968:
quote.text: The image of the affected eye is clearer and in consequence the diplopy more striking the less the cast of the eye; hence the double vision will be noticed by the patient before the misdirection of the eye attracts the attention of those about him.

quote.citation: 2011, Thomas Penn, Winter King, Penguin, published 2012, page 7:
quote.text: Arriving in Brittany, the Woodville exiles found a sallow young man, with dark hair curled in the shoulder-length fashion of the time and a penchant for expensively dyed black clothes, whose steady gaze was made more disconcerting by a cast in his left eye – such that while one eye looked at you, the other searched for you.

definitions.definition: Visual appearance.

quote.citation: 2004, Betsy Brill, Photojournalism: The Professional's Approach‎[2], page 240:
quote.text: Using a tungsten-balanced film outdoors results in a blue cast to the photo.

quote.citation: 2007, Lindsay Armstrong, The Australian's Housekeeper Bride‎[3], page 78:
quote.text: He stared down at his champagne glass with narrowed eyes and a hard cast to his mouth.

definitions.definition: The form of one's thoughts, mind etc.

quote.citation: 1894, Wilson Lloyd Bevan, Sir William Petty : A Study in English Economic Literature, page 40:
quote.text: The cast of mind which prompted the plan was permanent, and in it are to be found both the strength and the weakness of Petty's character.

quote.citation: 1928 February, H[oward] P[hillips] Lovecraft, “The Call of Cthulhu”, in Farnsworth Wright, editor, Weird Tales: A Magazine of the Bizarre and Unusual, volume 11, number 2, Indianapolis, Ind.: Popular Fiction Pub. Co., →OCLC, pages 159–178 and 287:
quote.text: Young Wilcox’s rejoinder, which impressed my uncle enough to make him recall and record it verbatim, was of a fantastically poetic cast which must have typified his whole conversation, and which I have since found highly ​characteristic of him.

quote.citation: 1992, Hilary Mantel, A Place of Greater Safety, Harper Perennial, published 2007, page 330:
quote.text: I have read all her articles and come to admire both her elegant turn of phrase and the noble cast of mind which inspires it; but never, I confess, did I look to see beauty and wit so perfectly united.

definitions.definition: Obsolete form of caste (“hereditary social class of South Asia”).

quote.citation: 1821, Report of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, volumes 12-16, page 160:
quote.text: The brahmin's cast is higher than any other cast.

definitions.definition: Animal and insect remains which have been regurgitated by a bird.
A group of crabs.
(firearms) The measurement of the angle of a shotgun stock from a top-view center line, used to align the shotgun to the shooter's eye.

quote.citation: Savage Arms, "THE PERFECT SHOTGUN FIT," 2021
quote.text: Cast is the measurement of the central line of the gun and the stock’s butt. If the butt is tilted slightly to the left of the central line, it’s called “cast on.” If the butt is tilted slightly to the right of the central line, it’s called “cast off.”

definitions.definition: A chance or attempt at something.
(archaic, colloquial) Assistance given by transporting a person or lightening their labour.

quote.citation: 1852, Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, volumes 17-18, page 398:
quote.text: The superiors rode în a spring-van, and the rest in the wagon, while I walked the whole distance. None of them had the civility to give me a cast forward on either vehicle,  […]

quote.citation: 1882, Sir James William Redhouse, The Turkish Vade-Mecum of Ottoman Colloquial Language, page 328:
quote.text: boatman, just give us a cast over to the other side of the water.

definitions.definition: Of an animal, such as a horse or sheep: Lying in a position from which it cannot rise on its own.
